name: Bianca Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lay out fittings and read the job sheet before we take the truck out, then I work with the lead on repairs and new connections. I like getting the right part onto the right pole; I still need her to check my finished joints, which can be humbling after a long day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the small changes sound fine if the parts list is accurate and a person still signs a repair. I sometimes use an AI tool to put a rough maintenance note into plain words, but I check the pole number myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still learning, and I notice every time my lead has to correct how I wrap a connection. Our mortgage and two children's expenses leave us about three and a half months saved, so even with steady line work I don't feel rich in options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and have my lead check my final connections until I can do them cleanly. In the first year I'd stop dipping into savings for small weekend outings and put 20 from each pay into the house repair account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels ordinary, in a way that is almost a relief. The house still needs a roof repair, so I would not call the family finances carefree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you saving for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damp patch over our back room gets bigger after hard rain. My partner measured it last weekend, and I want the roofer's estimate covered without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare the tool's polished sentence to the location and parts written on my glove card. The AI note-writing tool once swapped north and south, which would have sent a crew to the wrong side of the street.

say: I would accept **small paperwork help** if a person still signs each repair.
I would check every **pole number** before using an AI-polished note.
think: I am still learning **clean connections** and depend on lead checks.
Our **three-and-a-half-month cushion** has to cover the mortgage and children.
do: Keep **line shifts** and ask the lead to check final connections.
Put **20 per pay** into a house repair account.
feel: Relieved about work, but aware of the **roof bill**.
S0.quote: The AI note-writing tool once swapped north and south, which would have sent a crew to the wrong side of the street.
fieldNote: She uses AI occasionally for wording but checks it against a **glove card** after catching a directional error.
Her moderate savings are allocated toward a **roof repair**, making the plateau financially less comfortable than it sounds.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and request lead checks on final connections
Put 20 from each pay into the house repair account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office and the crews to test the new dispatch plans on actual faults before treating them as a finished product. The software can book jobs, but it doesn't know that the service road behind the old mill floods after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our hands stay useful for a while, though a leaner planning office could make the field shifts chaotic. I could be the junior sent home first if a smarter schedule squeezes more work from fewer crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the dispatcher to show me how job tickets are made and compare three recent tickets with what we found on site. If the new system comes in, I'd learn the approved routing screen after the senior crew has tested it, and I'd ask another utility yard about openings if my days drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested, but I want proof from a wet Thursday, not a clean demonstration. The possibility of losing even one shift a week makes the mortgage feel louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as proof for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the route to get our truck to the correct access gate and list the right switch before anyone leaves the yard. I'd keep the three tickets with dates so the supervisor can see a pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a complaint with coworkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the mistakes to the supervisor with the dispatcher, because she can explain why the original route was chosen. If the company fixes them, I'd happily use the system.

say: I would ask crews and dispatchers to test **real fault routes**.
I would judge the system by **correct access and switches**.
think: I could lose **one paid shift** if scheduling reduces crew hours.
I fear a smaller planning office could make **field work chaotic**.
do: Compare **three job tickets** with what crews found on site.
Learn the **approved routing screen** after senior crews test it.
Ask another **utility yard** about openings if days fall.
feel: Interested in evidence, but **anxious** about lost shifts.
S1.quote: I want proof from a wet Thursday, not a clean demonstration.
fieldNote: She defines proof through **access and switches**, with dated tickets as evidence.
Her response to risk is measured: learn the **tested screen** and inquire about other work only if shifts fall.

steps.text: Compare three recent job tickets with on-site findings
Learn the approved routing screen after senior crew tests
Ask another utility yard about openings if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI in 2028 would alter planning before any machine could fix our overhead lines. I'd ask for the company's crew forecast and safety rules in writing, since robots able to do the physical repairs come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 when the office changes and 48 at the robot date. Our children will still be in school, and I can't turn the roof fund into mortgage payments for more than a few months if line shifts vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the roof estimate now and cancel the paid sports channel until we know the company's plan. In 2029 I'd keep taking repair shifts, check computer job tickets with the lead, and apply to the transit maintenance depot if line hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That short warning worries me more than the machine itself. I can handle a hard week, but I cannot build a new income in two years just by being willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the transit depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They maintain overhead power for the buses, so some of my certificate might carry across. I would need to ask about supervision and an actual paid place before changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after the estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the number rather than hide it and suggest we fix the leak before spending on anything extra. If the price is too high, we would ask the roofer what part has to be done first.

say: I would separate **2028 planning** changes from 2031 physical robots.
I would request a written **crew forecast** and safety rules.
think: I will be **45 and 48** at the two dates.
Our school-age children, roof and **mortgage** outlast a short savings cushion.
do: Get the **roof estimate** and cancel the sports channel now.
Keep **repair shifts** in 2029 and check job tickets.
Apply to **transit maintenance** if line hours fall.
feel: Worried by the **short warning**, though still looking for options.
S2.quote: I cannot build a new income in two years just by being willing.
fieldNote: She grounds the fast scenario in a pending **roof estimate** and a mortgage, not abstract fear.
Her possible transit move uses an **overhead power connection** but depends on a paid vacancy and supervision.

steps.text: Cancel the paid sports channel until crew plans are clear
Keep repair shifts and check computer tickets in 2029
Apply to transit maintenance if line hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my coworkers that five years is enough to measure how the office system affects crew hours and correct it. I'd want a joint safety review before robots take on line repairs around 2034, not an announcement after the timetable is set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when the thinking work changes, I'll have more time to build a house fund than in the fast case. I'll be 51 when robots can repair lines, and my children will be older but the mortgage and any further study costs will still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask which switching qualification the utility will pay for and keep saving 20 per pay for the roof. If a funded place opens, I'd enrol; in 2032 I'd continue line shifts and apply for a paid switching position after passing the assessment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is room to breathe, but I'd still be looking at the assessment date on the calendar. I'm willing to learn proven procedures, though I don't want to gamble the roof fund on an untested course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is switching work in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means isolating the right part of the network before a crew touches it, with someone experienced checking my work while I learn. I'm not claiming I could isolate a power line safely on my own tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your lead support the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask her to show me the errors she sees in trainees and whether graduates actually get paid shifts. Her answer would matter more than the brochure.

say: I would measure the office system against **crew hours** over five years.
I would ask for a **joint safety review** before 2034 robots.
think: I will be **48 then 51** at the two arrival dates.
Our older children, mortgage and **roof costs** still constrain a career move.
do: Ask about a **funded switching** qualification and save 20 per pay.
Enrol if funded and continue **line shifts** in 2032.
Apply for **paid switching work** after passing.
feel: More room to breathe, with a keen eye on the **assessment date**.
S3.quote: I'm not claiming I could isolate a power line safely on my own tomorrow.
fieldNote: She sees switching as a **specific safety skill**, not a vague escape from physical line work.
Her willingness to train depends on **funding and paid shifts**, while savings remain earmarked for the roof.

steps.text: Save 20 each pay toward the roof repair
Enrol in switching qualification if the utility funds it
Apply for paid switching work after passing assessment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time for the company to show working results and include the people who use the equipment. I'd ask for annual numbers on crew hours and faults, since a promise in 2026 is hard to check in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and 56 when capable robots reach line repairs in 2039. The children may be grown, but I have not seen a pension figure or a mortgage balance that would let me simply stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with the line crew while I learn, finish paying for the roof, and add 20 to the mortgage payment each pay once the repair is covered. If the utility funds switching training I'd take it, then in 2037 I'd apply for a paid network switching post if qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The decade feels manageable because I can take one measured step at a time. I would still be unsettled if the only plan for experienced workers was to watch robots from a yard without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual numbers tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for whether fewer people are paid to do the same number of repairs, not just whether outages fell. If hours start slipping, I'd ask about switching vacancies sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could retirement at 56 be an option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps, but I'd need actual benefit statements and a cleared mortgage before saying so. I would plan on paid work rather than ask the children to cover us.

say: I would ask for yearly **crew-hour and fault** figures during the decade.
I would judge promised benefits by **working results**, not a distant pledge.
think: I will be **53 and 56** at the two arrival dates.
I cannot assume a pension or paid-off **mortgage** will replace wages.
do: Stay with the **line crew** while clearing the roof bill.
Add **20 to mortgage payments** once the repair is funded.
Take funded **switching training** and apply in 2037 if qualified.
feel: Able to take measured steps, while uneasy about **unpaid displacement**.
S4.quote: I would plan on paid work rather than ask the children to cover us.
fieldNote: She uses **annual crew-hour figures** to judge whether automation is eroding paid work before robot arrival.
Her ten-year money plan moves from the **roof bill** to mortgage principal, with switching only after funded training.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts while the roof repair is funded
Add 20 to mortgage payments after the roof is covered
Take funded switching training if offered
Apply for paid switching work in 2037 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the roof and mortgage do not wait while I find another paid role. Written crew forecasts, honest equipment trials and funded training with real vacancies would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what proof the company would give us each year. I would want hours and safety incidents on the same page, because a faster repair is no victory if the crews lose their pay.

headlineQuote: I would want hours and safety incidents on the same page, because a faster repair is no victory if the crews lose their pay.
portrait: Bianca is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** sharing a mortgage and two school-age children with her partner.
Her household has about **3.5 months** saved, with a roof repair still to fund.
She uses AI occasionally for notes but checks **pole details** against her own field record.
She seeks **proved tools** and funded switching training while tracking actual crew hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because the mortgage and roof bill leave little time for a job change.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written forecasts**, honest trials and funded training linked to paid vacancies.
